summary: Heiner Eichner was a linguist and Indologist who studied at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg under Karl Hoffmann (~1964–1974). He later held a post at the University of Vienna from ~1989 to 2010.
Heinrich August Eduard Schaeffer worked in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Leipzig and served as Principal at the Evangelical Lutheran Central High School.

Heinrich August Jäschke was a scholar in Tibetology and linguistics. He studied at Pädagogium Niesky and Gnadenfeld Theological Seminary, later serving at Pädagogium Niesky (1842–1856), Moravian Mission, Kyelang (1856–1863), and Moravian Church (1857–1868).

Heinrich Blatt was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Munich, Leipzig, Berlin, Würzburg, and Erlangen-Nuremberg (Ph.D. 1923). He served as a librarian at Würzburg University Library from 1923 to 1946.

Heinrich Blochmann worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, Indology, and history and archaeology. He studied at Leipzig, Paris, and Calcutta, and held posts at Doveton College (1862–1864), Aliah University (1860, 1865, 1870), and The Asiatic Society (1868–1878).
Heinrich Brunn was a scholar in history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Bonn (~1839–1843) and held a post at the University of Munich from ~1865 to 1894.

Heinrich Düntzer specialized in linguistics and Indology, studying at the University of Bonn and under Franz Bopp in Berlin. He held posts at the University of Bonn (~1836–1846) and as a librarian at Dreikönigsgymnasium (1846–1885).

Heinrich Ewald was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Göttingen under Thomas Christian Tychsen. He was a professor at Göttingen (1824–1837, 1848–1867) and held a post at the University of Tübingen (1838–1848).

Heinrich Franz Joseph Junker specialized in Iranian, Central Asian, and linguistic studies. After completing his Ph.D. under Christian Bartholomae at Heidelberg, he held professorships at Giessen, Hamburg, Leipzig (1926–1945), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1951).
Heinrich Gustav Hotho was a scholar of philosophy who studied at Humboldt University of Berlin from ~1820 to 1826. He subsequently held a post at Humboldt University of Berlin from ~1828 to 1873.
Heinrich Gössel worked in the field of Indology. He studied at the University of Leipzig under Ernst Windisch (~1906–1912), where he also held an assistant post in 1917.

Heinrich Hackmann worked in sinology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Leipzig, Göttingen, and Basel, later serving as privatdozent at Göttingen (~1893–1894) and professor of History of Religions at the University of Amsterdam (1913–1934).

Heinrich Hettrich was a scholar of linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Saarland, Giessen, and Munich, later holding posts at Salzburg, Zurich, Marburg, and the University of Würzburg as chair from 1989.

Heinrich Hübschmann was a linguist, Iranianist, and Indologist. He studied under August Schleicher at Jena and Martin Haug at Munich, later working as a privatdozent at Leipzig (1875) and professor of comparative linguistics at Strasbourg (1877).

Heinrich Kiepert was a scholar of history, archaeology, and geography. He studied at Berlin and Jena, and later served at the Geographisches Institut Weimar (1845–1852) and as professor of geography at Humboldt University of Berlin (1859, 1874).

Heinrich Leberecht Fleischer worked in linguistics and Oriental studies. He studied at Leipzig and in Paris under Silvestre de Sacy, Caussin de Perceval, Chézy, and Jaubert, and held the chair of Oriental languages at Leipzig from 1836.

Heinrich Lüders was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Munich and Göttingen under Franz Kielhorn. He held a chair at Humboldt University of Berlin (1909–1935) and served as secretary of the Prussian Academy of Sciences (1920–1938).

Heinrich Meinhard was an Indologist and anthropologist who completed his Ph.D. under Willibald Kirfel at Bonn. He served at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin (~1928–1937), Pitt Rivers Museum (1938–1947), and Durham University (1950).

Heinrich Meyer-Benfey was an Indologist and Germanist who studied at the University of Göttingen (~1888–1895). He later served at the University of Hamburg as a privatdozent (1919) and associate professor of German (1923–1938).

Heinrich Nau was an Indologist who studied at the University of Marburg, Concordia Seminary (~1901–1905), and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1914–1920), where he earned his Ph.D. under Eugen Hultzsch.
